entries.title: Here’s What the AI Apocalypse Could Look Like
entries.summary: This week on “Uncanny Valley,” we discuss three possible AI doomsday scenarios, AI safety, and the unexpected bipartisan alliance forming against AI.
entries.content:
The debate of whether AI can kill us has been everywhere lately, but what would an actual AI catastrophe look like? This week, Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger break down three real-world scenarios experts worry the most about—including hacked water supplies, bioweapons, and autonomous robots. We also discuss the highlights of Salesforce’s annual conference, where OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei defended their positions on AI safety. Plus, Leah tells us how this backlash against AI has become a rare bipartisan flash point, to the point that Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon shared a stage over it this week.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

  • China Isn’t Buying Silicon Valley’s Call for an AI Slowdown
  • Washington Won’t Be Regulating AI Anytime Soon
  • Why So Many AI Researchers Think the Machines Could Kill Everyone
  • OpenAI Wants to Know if an AI Industry Slowdown Would Even Be Legal

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at [email protected].

Transcript

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Zoë Schiffer: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Brian Barrett: I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Zoë Schiffer: Today on the show, we're diving into the debate about whether AI is going to kill us all. And instead of just adding to the pile of hot takes that already exist, we're going to walk you through real, specific scenarios to the best of our ability about how AI would actually do this, and why the tech CEOs and politicians cannot seem to agree on the way forward. OK, guys, so the debate about AI safety has officially escaped containment.

Brian Barrett: Oh.

Zoë Schiffer: I know.

Brian Barrett: Zoë, I see what you did there. Wow.

Zoë Schiffer: You see what I did there? That's the thing that's really spread uncontrollably. AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and posted on X that, "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown. They call this, "pacing the frontier." And Sam Altman and Elon Musk have actually signed on, a rare moment of agreement. But honestly, with all of this talk about AI wiping out humanity, I have been left with a very basic question, which is, how exactly does this happen? What does AI going completely rogue actually look like?

Leah Feiger: I'm so happy we're doing this. We had such a great podcast last week with WIRED's Will Knight talking about everyone being concerned about this, but I want like a breakdown. I need you to just take me through every single scenario from bioweapons to nuclear codes, to what are we really talking about here when we're talking about AI deathbots.

Zoë Schiffer: We are going to do our very best. I did spend the most time I've ever spent reading LessWrong over the last two days trying to figure this out. They love a scenario-planning exercise, but just to get everyone up to speed on kind of the latest, there was an event this week hosted by Salesforce where Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, and NVIDIA's Jensen Huang were all in attendance, and naturally they had to talk about AI safety. Let's take a listen at what Sam Altman had to say.

Sam Altman, archival audio: I think the world is right to be afraid of this. So we have these two big challenges. We have the potential of a loss-of-control accident or some other serious thing that could go wrong. We have the potential of way too much power concentration and people fear that those developing AI could exert their worldview. And there is this sort of narrow path we have to navigate with pragmatism, with steadiness, with the ability for the world to trust that we'll make dependable decisions, consistent decisions through this. And I think people are saying, "Well, this now seems pretty important. Let's get it right."

Leah Feiger: I'm definitely in the camp that says we should be very concerned about this technology, how it's getting regulated, how it's getting utilized, the people in control. I don't disagree. And on the other hand, this also just reads like a fever-dream pitch to someone's massive IPO in the making.

Brian Barrett: I don't know. I get the marketing argument, but I think we're past that a little bit. I feel like—

Leah Feiger: Really?

Brian Barrett: If anything, well, if anything, Sam Altman has been using "the existential threat" as a reason not to go public yet. He's saying, "No, this is too dangerous. We have to wait until next year." Is that really why? I don't know, but there are probably some business reasons, too. I get why Anthropic and others saying, "Look, we're building something that's basically as strong as a nuclear weapon," felt like marketing. Something that's like, "Oh, actually I'm quitting because I think that I'm building something that will actually destroy the world," feels different. I feel like there's a substantive difference.

Leah Feiger: The quitting part feels different to me, but this is still Sam Altman. His financial future is on the line here with this and it's hard ... At least it's hard for me to parse that as being a way. "We are building the biggest, bestest, most powerful robot ever, and you guys should be kind of scared about it. And don't worry, we're going to take steps. They're not going to be regulatory steps, but there'll be steps of some kind." That still feels like a marketing ploy in some worlds.

Brian Barrett: I guess. I guess the nature of the threat, though, and we'll get into that later, is more that like, "Oh, we don't know how to control these things. They're going to go nuts and we're not going to be able to stop it." That feels like, "We're not competent enough right now to do anything about it," which feels like less of a marketing-

Leah Feiger: That's fair. What did everyone else at the seminar say, Zoë?

Zoë Schiffer: So Dario was introduced by Salesforce's CEO, Marc Benioff, who is very laissez-faire and does not seem worried about AI's existential risks.

Marc Benioff, archival audio: Dario, hello Dario. How are you?

Dario Amodei, archival audio: Hey.

Marc Benioff, archival audio: Great to have you. Fantastic. Great job, Dario. You're doing an amazing job leading the AI industry, guiding it all right from our Slack headquarters building. We watch you every day. Give us your state, where your mind is right now.

Dario Amodei, archival audio: Yeah, obviously it's very tempting to attack your competitor and say, "These guys are unsafe; we're safe." But I think the more responsible way to respond to it is to say, "Hey, first of all, let's look at our own record. We may not have had this big high-profile incident, but I'm sure we're not perfect. Let's look at everything, and we can always be better. Let's make our practices better." Then, let's organize the rest of the industry and say, "What can we do to set standards for everyone? What can we do to make everyone's standards better?" And then, finally, there should be an international component to it. And that's essentially the three-step plan that I laid out in the essay.

Brian Barrett: Two things. Two things real quick. One, Anthropic did have its own high-profile incident. An Anthropic agent—

Leah Feiger: I was going to say.

Brian Barrett: ... did like extensive social engineering to try to trick a GitHub ... try to put a bad pull request into a GitHub repo? Anthropic has its issues here. The other thing is, too, Dario has this three-step plan. We can talk about that a little bit more later, but one of the steps of the plan is like, figure out China TBD, in a way that's just so unhelpful.

Leah Feiger: International. International.

Zoë Schiffer: WIRED editor Louise Matsakis just published, I thought, a really good piece on this. The idea that Dario can say, "We need an international plan. We need to figure out China. We need to negotiate in some way so that China's on board with this slowdown. But the prerequisite to negotiation is that we have to make sure that we regulate access to Chinese models in a way that keeps US AI far ahead." And China's like, "That doesn't feel like a good negotiation."

Brian Barrett: Why would we do that, Dario? Why?

Leah Feiger: Truly in that 30-second spiel, I'm just recounting every single person that he's managed to piss off, which even referencing his paper, Donald Trump was incensed by it and looked at it as such a mechanism for slowdown, that it has possibly been a linchpin for halting any sort of regulation that would happen because he was so mad about it. I have to say, hats off, being able to piss off every single person, even those that are theoretically in your economic corner is, my God, chef's kiss, impressive.

Zoë Schiffer: OK. So to close out the CEO statements, Jensen Huang had some thought of his own, and it seems like something that they all agree on is that AI safety matters as long as the companies can dictate the terms.

Jensen Huang, archival audio: Well, safety is paramount. In a lot of ways, it's job one. If you build a product or a service and you're not confident in its functionality, capability, or safety, then don't release it. And so that's a very obvious thing to do. You pace yourself until you are confident you're releasing something that the market would appreciate. The market forces are already there. We don't need any new laws. We don't need any new regulations.

Leah Feiger: I love that Jensen has this role that he currently has. Nvidia wasn't always the glorious company that it is today, but now he can really sit up there and say, "Why would you ... "

Zoë Schiffer: The crux of this argument, the crux of so many of these arguments that are anti-regulation here is that we're supposed to be relying on people who are not elected to dictate everything involving this, that it will impact everyone's lives regardless if they're using these services or not.

Leah Feiger: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

Zoë Schiffer: The invisible hand of the market is going to figure it out.

Brian Barrett: Oh, Leah forgot about the invisible hand again. Common mistake.

Leah Feiger: I did. I always do. And I know, I feel like I say this every few weeks, but these are not elected officials. So the fact that they are actually playing such a significant role here continues to boggle the mind, which is why I know I also keep on about so much of this is a bipartisan issue. Being regulatory or anti-regulatory is not a Democratic/Republican divide at this moment in time.

Brian Barrett: Well, and they also haven't done a lot to engender trust up until this point, full stop, right? I always go back to Sam Altman is the same guy who thinks that everyone should scan their eyeball into an orb, because eventually we're going to need eye-scanning orbs to create a new economy out of the ashes of—

Leah Feiger: Nothing incenses Brian Barrett like the orb.

Brian Barrett: The orb. I am obsessed with the orb. I think people forget the orb guy is the same guy as the AI guy, and I think holding those two in my brain at the same time makes every part of me hurt.

Zoë Schiffer: This kind of brings us to the how-is-it-actually-going-to-kill-us story, which is, a lot of these statements, in my opinion, boil down to, this could be really bad and we should do something about it. But I'm like, what specifically are you saying could happen? And I feel like there's kind of three scenarios roughly that this falls into. AI starts hacking things. It's actually already started, and both Anthropic and OpenAI have had very high-profile incidents where the agents escaped control and hacked into other systems without the knowledge of researchers, and it was discovered later what had happened. AI creates a novel bioweapon, and that weapon is released to the public in a way that is nearly impossible to control and it kills everyone. And then there's kind of the vague AI just escapes control. It starts acting on its own. It doesn't listen to our instructions, and we don't know what could happen, but we can't do anything about it and that's scary.

Leah Feiger: OK. This is super helpful for me that we're dividing it into these three categories.

Zoë Schiffer: I love a bucket.

Leah Feiger: I love a bucket. I want to go through every single one of these. My first question I suppose is, where do the nuclear codes getting pressed, which bucket do they fall into?

Brian Barrett: That's the one that we actually don't have to worry about, right?

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah.

Leah Feiger: Tell me more.

Zoë Schiffer: You talk to AI researchers, and if you really, really press them, you can get to the three buckets that I just laid out. But then if you keep talking to them, they'll be like, "Well, there are these other scenarios where AI is in a robot, the robot is walking around, and then the robot can interact with the physical world in a way that's really, really scary." But that's a little further away, and they'll admit it's a little more far-fetched.

Brian Barrett: So I think one thing, Zoë, in terms of your buckets, that I want to carve out maybe a sub-bucket or a little pail within a bucket.

Zoë Schiffer: Wow, a pail.

Brian Barrett: No, because you were saying AI creates a bioweapon, AI hacks something, AI whatever, all of which: true. But I think there's a distinction between human-guided things happening there versus AI doing it on its own. I think a lot of people are like, "Oh, how would AI release a bioweapon? That's crazy." Which is, yeah, sure, fine. But there are also bad people in the world who might use AI to make a bioweapon and then release it, right?

Zoë Schiffer: Oh, well, I mean, that scenario is one that I think is totally valid. To me, if you say giving people access to information about how to create a bioweapon, someone is going to be dumb enough and reckless enough to actually do it. I'm like, no, totally. People are doing all sorts of horrible, dangerous, malicious things all the time.

Leah Feiger: With inspiration from the internet.

Zoë Schiffer: Right. I buy that that is really, really dangerous. AI doing it completely on its own, again, we'll talk about the scenario, but that seems to me a little more far-fetched.

Brian Barrett: I'm probably going to get pilloried for this, but I do want to take us back to the 1983 film, WarGames.

Leah Feiger: No, this is exactly what I think we should be talking about. This is my ... Yes. WarGames is the ... Yes.

Brian Barrett: Because here's the thing, AI is not going to be pushing the button or turning the keys or whatever, but in WarGames, which is about AI basically, a computer almost kicking off nuclear war, it's more that it made the US think that it was under attack by Soviet nuclear weapons. And so is there a risk then, I assume, I would hope, I'm not an expert here, that we have enough safeguards in place that that would not actually happen here, and we have enough satellite technology to be able to confirm various things. It's fine. But I think the vector that's probably of concern would be AI triggering some sort of alert that causes a catastrophic series of events.

Leah Feiger: OK. I'm so happy you brought up WarGames. Everyone's been … It's Michael Creighton this and Jurassic Park that, but no, no, no. To me, it is very much all about, almost like the teaching scenario, which is how so many of these hacks occurred before, like the unanswerable question, how do I get to the bottom of this information that made these agents act the way that they did? We're being told. To take us even further back in history, because I can't help myself, when I'm thinking of the way in which nations communicate, and it's changed very, very much over the years. Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria shot and killed in Sarajevo in 1914. People were marching before that for World War I. Everyone was already on the march. And so the way that antagonistic nations are communicating with each other in already times of stress to have this additional war-game scenario, or this agent thought that we were doing this, so went down this path. I don't know. I'm aware that I'm very much sounding like an insane doomer right now, but these are the things that I'm thinking about, which is, will we actually use our satellites and contact Russia or whomever before getting into attack mode? Will Trump send out a Truth Social post before anything has been confirmed? Will state secrets be shared in public by Kash Patel? I have so many questions about how, maybe even specifically our current administration would be able to deal with a scenario like that, and we're just being told to hold on, wait a second. A couple of very, very wealthy men who have done some very impressive businesses have got it under control.

Brian Barrett: We've got so many tinderboxes too that are sort of ready to be set off, whether it's Ukraine, whether it's Iran, whether it's China, the conditions are ripe for something not to go great, whether that ends all humanity or sparks just an endless series of devastating wars, who can say? Zoë, what's another scenario you got?

Zoë Schiffer: When I was trying to get to what concretely would happen, two things that people brought up were, AI is used or AI breaks into on its own a water facility, changes the chemicals in a way that's really dangerous to humans and basically poisons the water supply for major cities across the US. Earlier this year, I think nine Mexican government organizations, like utilities were hacked, and there was a big cyber report that I read yesterday about this where Claude was used to plan the attack and build some of the tools. Ultimately, experts said AI didn't invent a new kind of attack, but it made the attack a lot cheaper and faster to execute. This comes just as the FBI in July put out a warning that utilities companies in the United States were being targeted. So again, this isn't one where AI on its own is necessarily doing things, but I think the fear is, this is already happening with bad actors, bad human actors in the loop, and if you have agents that can act of their own accord, this would be something we would be worried about.

Brian Barrett: You're right that it is file under things that are already happening. In the US, it was a dozen US states, at least that we know of, that around linked hackers were at least probing the water supply there, the industrial controls. To your point, I do think it's the kind of thing where does that end all of humanity? Probably not, not all at once, but there's a lot of water supplies out there. I think the same thing goes for power grids. People have been probing power grid vulnerabilities for a long time. AI could probably do that more efficiently, more quickly, and cause some real harm.

Leah Feiger: I also wonder how quickly rollbacks on this would be able to happen. Even stuff that's not AI. We've talked a lot, to Zoë's dismay about Cyclospora outbreaks across the US over this past summer. That was not AI—

Brian Barrett: Thank you for introducing turbo diarrhea.

Leah Feiger: I'm never going to miss a chance not to, but it's really ... That wasn't AI. That wasn't AI at all. And the idea that the US government and health departments were kind of ill-equipped to respond to something in that kind is a little concerning when we're looking at additional bad actors entering the mix.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. And that naturally segues into bioweapons. This is something that's brought up a lot when you talk about possible AI doomsday scenarios. The idea is that AI is used to create and deploy a novel bioweapon. Often they'll say things like, they'll modify an existing pathogen in a way that existing treatments can't work on it. So it's a bioweapon that we basically can't combat in any known way immediately. And the idea is that AI can actually figure out how you deploy this to people, can evade detection. It had ideas for how to get it through airport security and whatnot. So one thing that I realized in having some of these conversations and reading is that the bioweapons category is a little bit vague on purpose because scientists are legitimately worried that if they give people too much information about how to use chatbots in this way or how agents could do this supposedly on their own, that will create some of these kind of doomsday scenarios. But the idea, again, is AI either on its own or with a human in the loop is able to do this.

Leah Feiger: I'm fascinated by the point that scientists are saying that they actually don't even want to provide ideas here.

Brian Barrett: And I'll say too, this is another ... I keep following things in this category, things that are already maybe potentially happening. Anthropic's risk report from about a week ago said that they had blocked people who were potentially trying to do this already. It's a real active concern. Although again, yeah, I agree with everybody that an Optimus bot is not going to be in a lab cooking up anthrax. Not yet.

Zoë Schiffer: OK. So the third category is AI escapes human control. Already, some people who are working on these systems are saying we are losing the ability to see and study what the agents are doing in certain scenarios. They're already pretty good at evading detection. I was really struck in the METR report on OpenAI's Hugging Face incident that their investigation seemed to rely in large part on looking at the AI's chain of thought, asking the AI certain questions. Obviously, I guess they were using AI to investigate the AI, but the idea is that the agents stop listening to humans entirely. They start pursuing "their own aims and goals" and we don't know what those could be. The paperclip idea is brought up a lot in this scenario, if anyone remembers.

Brian Barrett: So the paperclip problem predates LLMs by about a decade. It was a philosopher named Nick Bostrom at the University of Oxford, and his thought experiment was this. Basically, let's say you have an AI and its only task is to produce paperclips. It's just like, "Hey AI, your job is to make paperclips." It's going to want to do that, and it's going to figure out ways to do that, and it's going to keep doing it over and over again until the world is totally overrun by paperclips, then we're all buried in an avalanche of paperclips because a superintelligent AI will stop at nothing to achieve its task. It sounds silly. It is, but also it's very prescient, I think, because this is exactly what happened with the OpenAI incidents. Yeah, these are AI agents who were given a job and they were so hell-bent on executing that task that they broke every other rule, they deceived, they coordinated, they did all these things in pursuit of their original task. So the concern is that we'll have a superintelligent AI that's given a task and it decides that the only way to complete that task is to destroy all humans, whatever it is. And it's because it's superintelligent, who knows what it will devise, because we aren't smart enough to figure that out. That part I'm a little bit less sold on, but you can see, if not how the result happens, you can see how the impetus happens. You can see the catalyst of it, which is AI is given a task or gives itself a task and all hell breaks loose.

Leah Feiger: And this kind of brings us to some of the other voices in the AI safety debate who are saying that we should be focusing on the current risks, like some of those that you've just laid out that have already been happening rather than speculating about the future ones. Even if the paperclip scenario is this outlandish thing, we have already experienced different flavors of that. This week, WIRED's Lauren Goode spoke with Timnit Gebru, a computer scientist who says we're asking the wrong questions and that the debate is a kind of a distraction from harms that are already happening, including autonomous weapons and warfare, AI's role in climate change, labor displacement, AI-assisted attempts to build weapons that Anthropic says it's already blocked, like you've mentioned. There's a lot of really interesting things in here that, I don't know. I think I agree with the very nitty-gritties of, yes, we have to be talking about these specific things, while simultaneously I'm OK using the paperclip scenario to say, "OK, this is happening. Where could it take us next?"

Brian Barrett: It's also, and we talked about this with Will a little bit last week, but I still can't get over, the thing that everyone seems to be most worried about is this idea of recursive self-improvement where AI starts building the next AI. An AI model builds the next AI model and so on and so forth until you get this exponential progress in AI and we don't know how it works anymore, we don't know how to control it. And I'm a simpleton, I'm a simple guy, but why not just don't do that? Why not just don't do that? How about that? If we're all so worried about that, how about we just don't? Zoë, you can yell at me now, but why don't we just not?

Zoë Schiffer: OK. No, no, no, no. I don't want to yell. I just want to go back to something Leah said at the very top, which is how much of this is marketing. I just think it's so baffling to me that we were all talking about AGI for so long, and that was the big milestone and the big thing that everyone was heading toward, and we had to get to AGI before China and blah, blah, blah. And then all of a sudden RSI just kind of replaced it because AGI didn't seem as likely. And now RSI is being used in very, very, very similar ways. It's like, actually, this is the thing that's going to be really scary, and we need to get to this milestone before China. I'm just like, are we just going to keep coming up with scary three-letter acronyms to talk about AI's power in a way that makes regulation less likely and AI investment a lot more likely?

Leah Feiger: Zoë, everything you just said, I couldn't agree with you more. Wow. Wow.

Brian Barrett: When really, the real three-letter acronym is IPO. Huh? Did that work? Did I do it?

Zoë Schiffer: Wow.

Brian Barrett: Is that something?

Leah Feiger: I didn't know where you were going.

Zoë Schiffer: Trying to get in on this.

Leah Feiger: You just want to be part of this.

Brian Barrett: Successfully. What do you mean? Trying to get in on it. Succeeding.

Leah Feiger: I mentioned this a little bit earlier in the episode, but I want to get back to it, which is, the US government's response to all of this and some odd alliances that are occurring as a result. WIRED's Hugo Lowell in our Inner Loop newsletter talks about how there's basically no legislation that's likely going to be coming down the pike this year, partially because of slowdowns in Congress and also because the Trump administration is just pretty much not interested in regulation. Donald Trump keeps getting personal phone calls from all sorts of Silicon Valley leaders who are saying this, that, and the other thing. As a result, Trump's Truth Social recently has just been littered with mentions of, "We are not doing this. We're not losing to China. We're not slowing down." All to say, like I mentioned earlier, this is not a partisan issue, so you have some folks from very different camps that are getting into bed together over this. On Tuesday at a event called the Pro-Human Assembly in Washington, DC, Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon shared a stage where they denounced tech oligarchs and called for reining in AI before it exceeds human control. Look, they've both been saying these things separately for a while. That's not new information. The fact that both of them thought that it was a good idea and high time for them to get on stage together fascinated me. Again, we already knew how they felt about this. To do it together, fascinating. Bannon's proposals very much differ from Sanders. He doesn't trust Congress. He wants Trump to slow development, executive order, et cetera, et cetera. Sanders is a man of the people, really wants some congressional oversight here. But there were some really interesting things that came up in this conference that I'm still thinking about, again, on stage with both of these people. The conference included parents whose teenagers had died by suicide after chatbot relationships, talks about child safety regulation, AI-generated nonconsensual sexual imagery. There was a lot of stuff which would be totally normal and not out of place on one of these stages, but again, it was all of these people together. And Trump meanwhile is just continuing to slow down all of this. He posted that the "only controls or guardrails that AI needs is a capitalized strong and smart (high IQ) president, and the USA has that in spades." So that's where we're at, folks.

Zoë Schiffer: I have two things to say. Number one, Steve Bannon, the only thing I want to hear from you is the unreleased audio from your All-In episode that never occurred. Please, God, someone send it to me. Number two, have any of these people articulated why China winning the AI race is so ... Are they worried that China's hacking abilities get so good and scary or that Chinese AI proliferates and influences America and everyone turns communist? What's the scenario?

Brian Barrett: I think it's more simple than that, maybe. I think it's economic. I think that so much of the US economy is propped up on AI right now that if China becomes the world leader in AI and our industry crumbles because of that, we're in trouble. I think there are also security concerns, but I think fundamentally, if the US is not the leader in AI, everything kind of crumbles economically.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, no, I get that. And again, we have talked about Chinese open models being very close to as good as some of the models from the leading US frontier labs, and obviously a lot cheaper if they're open source. I completely get that. I think I'm craving so much specificity in this conversation because I just feel like Dario, Sam, all of the politicians, they're so vague in how they talk about this and they've been doing it for so long, the threat of China in all of these different ways, the threat of RSI, AGI, that I'm like, "What actually are we talking about?"

Brian Barrett: I have one more thing on Trump. We're going to have a story from Maddy Varner, a WIRED senior writer about the dynamics here. But basically the reason that these AI labs are saying we're not sure if we can slow down, we're not sure if we can pace the frontier, is that we're worried that it will be an antitrust violation. We are worried that the FTC is going to come after us with an enforcement action because we are colluding, et cetera.

Leah Feiger: Now you're worried about an antitrust violation?

Brian Barrett: Yeah, but that's what they're saying. And Donald Trump has effectively turned every enforcement branch of the US government into his own personal attack dogs. So if Donald Trump is saying, "You need to keep building AI as fast as you can," and if these AI companies collectively say, "Actually, we're going to slow down," regardless of the merits of it, you could pretty easily see an antitrust case popping up real quick as a way to say, "No, you're not slowing down at all." So by making these overt threats on Truth Social, I think he is really making it very hard for these AI companies to do any kind of meaningful slowdown, any kind of pullback.

Leah Feiger: Coming up after the break, we'll share our WIRED TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us.

Zoë Schiffer: OK, it's time for our WIRED TIRED segment. As usual, whatever is new and cool is WIRED, whatever passé thing we're totally over is TIRED. Leah, do you want to go first?

Leah Feiger: OK. My TIRED is, while I often get really lovely comments on social media and emails from our avid readers and listeners about how much they love Wired.com and love Uncanny Valley, I also sometimes get emails from people who are asking me for specific information on logins and reading articles and accessing different WIRED bits and bobs. So that's my TIRED, getting those ... I'm sorry, if you message me and ask for help getting anything WIRED, Condé Nast, I have nothing. I don't know how to do it. I barely know how to use my own phone. So that's my TIRED.

Brian Barrett: Leave Leah alone. OK.

Leah Feiger: Leave me alone. My WIRED is we have a new app, and it is so beautiful. Just launched this week. Highly recommend checking it out, downloading it. As someone who really doesn't like adding additional little pieces, additional layers to my various routines, it's fantastic. It's really, really fantastic. It's so easy to use, connects so simply to subscriber everything. Highly recommend. I already love it. I have a feeling that this is going to change your life as well as mine, and no one will email me again.

Brian Barrett: It's a high part—

Zoë Schiffer: And Brian, what do you have?

Brian Barrett: My TIRED is, OK, it's not a new thing, but we talked about it today. AI lingo, AI industry lingo. I'm over it. I'm sorry. AI labs instead of companies. It's the frontier instead of just good tech. We're pacing it. We're pacing the frontier. What is that? Get it together. I know this has been part of the tech industry forever, right?

Leah Feiger: No, drag them. This is people who read too much Lord of the Rings and watched too much Star Trek who've tried to integrate cultural touchstones of their childhood into our day-to-day lives, and I hate it.

Brian Barrett: It's also a way to make it feel inaccessible, right? It's like, "Oh, they need to pace the frontier. Well, I don't know anything about that, but it sounds important. Oh, AI has an alignment problem. Oh, that sounds serious." It's really like AI's misbehaving. AI is not doing what you want it to. You don't have control over your stuff. So I am tired of it. That's my TIRED. My WIRED, Leah, you stole mine. I won't spend much time on it. The WIRED app, it is, it's great. A lot of work went into it. I have made my family members download it. They like it, or at least they tell me they do. So please go ahead and check it out and leave a review. It really helps.

entries.title: 26 Amazon Prime Perks You Might Know You Have (2026)
entries.summary: Your membership gets you more than free two-day shipping. Here’s what you may be missing ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days.
entries.content:
There’s a good chance that you initially purchased your Amazon Prime membership to get free two-day shipping. But there are dozens of additional perks that can be tricky to find—and considering the cost of an annual membership, you're doing yourself a disservice if you aren't taking advantage of all of them. I'm here to help you get your money's worth—especially ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days, which will run on October 6 and 7.

Below, I've listed the benefits you should be using as an Amazon Prime member. Arguably, these incentives alone aren't worth the cost of a membership, but chances are at least one of them will come in handy.

Amazon has had more than its fair share of debacles. But there are still an estimated 201 million members in the United States. If you're one of them, these perks are worth checking out.

Updated September 2026: I've ensured perks, coverage, pricing, and links are accurate ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days.

What’s Amazon Prime, and How Much Does It Cost?

Amazon Prime is a premium membership to Amazon.com. If you've never had a membership before, you can try it free for 30 days. This trial automatically renews, so set a reminder on your phone to reassess and make sure to cancel if you don't want to continue your membership.

Amazon Prime costs $139 per year. You can pay $15 per month instead, but that raises the cost of the membership to $180 annually, so you'll save more money by paying for the year up front. People 18 to 24 years old can get Prime for Young Adults (formerly called Prime Student), which is $69 annually or $7.50 per month after an extended six-month free trial. Prime for Young Adults has an exclusive cash-back program that lets members earn rewards on select purchases. Usually, they earn around 5 percent, but some shopping events bump up that rate.

Finally, some customers are eligible for Prime Access, a discounted Prime membership that cuts the subscription cost in half. If you verify that you receive qualifying SNAP benefits or other government assistance, you can get Amazon Prime for $7 per month. Note that Prime Access members have to reverify eligibility once per year, and can only use Prime Access for four years total before they need to choose a different membership.

Basic Amazon Prime Benefits

Prime members are eligible for free next-day shipping on millions of items and free two-day shipping on millions more. Depending on where you live, you may also be eligible for free same-day delivery or free Amazon Locker pickup. Other Amazon-owned stores also offer free and/or expedited shipping to Prime members, including ShopBop, Woot, and Zappos. Some merchants offer Buy With Prime at checkout, which lets you complete a purchase using your Amazon account instead of signing up for a new account entirely. It seems like more of a convenience than a benefit, but it may be appealing to some shoppers.

Prime members get free Amazon Music Prime, which pulls playlists and podcasts from a selection of 100 million songs and serves them ad-free. Members are also eligible for discounted subscriptions to Amazon Music Unlimited, a separate pick-and-play service like Apple Music or Spotify that offers on-demand access to 100 million songs. Normally, it costs $13 monthly, but Prime members can get it for $12 per month.

Prime Video is also included with your membership. There are some killer originals, like Fallout and The Expanse, in addition to other movies and shows. You can also stream sports on Prime Video, including NFL Thursday Night Football and select MMA fights. Purchased as a stand-alone subscription, Prime Video costs $9 per month. Note that, sadly, these plans include commercials. If you're a Prime member and you want to go ad-free, it'll cost another $5 per month.

Prime Day

I’d be remiss to gloss over Amazon’s members-only event, Prime Day. The semi-annual “holiday” has outperformed both Black Friday and Cyber Monday in years past, but not every Prime Day deal is actually a bargain. The WIRED Reviews team always covers the event to make good deals easier to find—our coverage is unique because we only write about deals on products we have personally tested and can verify are great buys, rather than flooding our roundups with questionable third-party brands. This year, Prime Big Deal Days will take place on October 6 and 7, following up the first Prime Day event that took place in June. Our team will cover the best-of-the-best deals throughout the event.

Exclusive Deals

Even outside of Prime Day, Amazon Prime members are eligible for special members-only discounts. You might be able to knock off a few bucks from your portable charger purchase, use a coupon on household essentials, or find lower prices on new Amazon devices. Individual discounts vary, but we see these sorts of promotions pretty frequently—and, as with Prime Day, not all of them are good.

Early-Access Lightning Deals

Both during and outside of special events like Prime Day, Black Friday, and Cyber Monday, Prime members get early access to select Lightning Deals. You'll be able to shop 30 minutes before other customers. Whether Lightning Deals are worth your money is another discussion entirely, but it's a perk worth checking out.

Amazon Day Delivery

Overwhelmed by the sheer number of boxes at your door? (Honestly, as a product reviewer, I feel that.) Amazon Day delivery lets you schedule all of your deliveries to arrive on a certain day of the week. Rather than dealing with a box or two at a time on multiple days, you can get one package with all of your orders on whatever day you prefer. If you use Amazon Day delivery, you aren't locked in. That means if you're ordering something you need quickly, you can still opt for the fastest shipping method. Amazon Day delivery is a good way to cut back on all that extra cardboard (and your carbon footprint).

No-Rush Rewards

If you don't need your order to arrive right away, sometimes at checkout you'll see the option for free No-Rush Shipping. You might get a free digital credit to use on things like ebooks or digital games, or you might get an instant discount off your order. (You can't choose which of the two you'll get.) Be aware that sometimes rewards expire after a certain duration.

Alexa+

Prime members get free access to Alexa+, which is the newest version of Amazon's voice assistant. It uses generative AI and costs $20 per month for non-Prime members. According to Amazon, you can talk naturally, phrase requests however you'd like, receive tailored recommendations based on your preferences, create bedtime stories, make smart shopping lists, and more.

Grubhub+

Amazon Prime members get free access to Grubhub+, which includes free delivery on some delivery orders, plus an assortment of Prime-exclusive discounts at a selection of restaurants throughout the year.

Amazon Fresh, Whole Foods, and Amazon Grocery

Amazon Fresh lets you order groceries via Amazon and get them delivered to your door. It's not available in all areas, but it is a different way to shop if you're trying to avoid in-person trips. You also get a selection of products from Whole Foods available through Amazon Fresh. If you're shopping at Whole Foods in person, you can scan the smartphone app to get an extra 10 percent off storewide sales and make use of other member discounts available throughout the year. There are also Prime-exclusive deals at Whole Foods every Tuesday and Friday.

There's a separate Amazon Grocery subscription that costs $10 a month or $100 a year. If you have SNAP or EBT benefits, you can get 50 percent off the monthly plan. This subscription gets you unlimited free grocery delivery on orders of $25 or more from Whole Foods Market, Amazon Fresh, and some local retailers.

Amazon Family

Amazon Family is a great way to share benefits among multiple people who live together. You can share certain benefits with one other adult in your household; up to four teens who were added before April 7, 2025; and up to four child profiles. Amazon no longer allows customers to add new teen accounts.

Amazon First Reads

Each month, Prime members can benefit from Amazon First Reads. You'll get at least one Kindle book from the selection for free. Nonmembers can get their two books for $2 apiece. As a reminder, you can read Kindle books even if you don't have a Kindle device, thanks to the free app available for phones and computers. (We also have a buying guide to help you pick the right Kindle.)

Prime Reading

In addition to First Reads, Prime members get access to tons of Kindle books via Prime Reading. There are more than a thousand items to choose from. Aside from books, you can access audiobooks and magazines, plus comics via Comixology.

Prime Gaming and Amazon Luna

Every month, Prime members are eligible for various rewards via Prime Gaming (formerly called Twitch Prime). The page redirects to Amazon Luna now, but you can still keep claiming your monthly rewards … you just also get access to Amazon Luna Standard, a cloud gaming service, if you want it. Amazon Luna gets you free access to many popular titles, though streaming games can be a little buggy. Prime Gaming includes in-game loot in a variety of popular games, free game downloads, free downloadable content (DLC) and expansions, premium currency, and more. You also get a free Twitch subscription, which are subscriptions to individual Twitch streamers (normally these “Twitch subs” cost money). With the free subscription you get from Amazon Prime, you can support channels you enjoy—creators make some money off the subscription, but it won't cost you anything extra.

$10 off Game Preorders

This discount used to be much better, but it's still worth looking into if you are in the market for a new video game. Occasionally, Prime members can receive $10 off when they preorder a game. Eligible titles show up here when they're available. Some video games also have free Release Day Delivery—just look for that shipping option when preordering a game.

Unlimited Online Photo Storage

Prime members get access to unlimited full-resolution photo storage, and 5 gigabytes of video storage as well. You can store, print, and share photos using the Amazon Photos app and back everything up to the cloud. (Printing is done through Shutterfly, where Prime members get a 45 percent discount and free shipping on orders over $35.) If your account ever loses Prime status, you'll need to pay at least $2 per month to keep storing your photos and videos, so this shouldn't be your primary backup method.

Discounted Amazon Kids+

Amazon Kids+ (formerly called FreeTime Unlimited) is Amazon's content service for kids. The service is compatible with several iOS, Android, and Amazon devices, like Fire tablets. It provides a bevy of parental controls while giving kiddos access to age-appropriate shows, books, games, and the like. Amazon Kids+ costs $8 per month, but Prime members can snag the subscription for $6 per month (or $79 and $48 per year, respectively).

Fuel Savings

By linking your Amazon Prime account to Earnify, a loyalty app owned by BP, you can save at least 10 cents per gallon on fuel at over 7,500 participating gas station locations.

Additional Perks for Specific Customers

Expecting a new addition to your family? Select Prime members can claim a free Baby Registry Welcome Box by creating a registry that has at least 10 unique items and $10 worth of purchases (by themselves or others). Learn more here.

Prime Rx offers select customers discounts on prescription medications. It's a prescription savings card that can be used at pharmacies nationwide, including Amazon Pharmacy. These savings programs are nothing new—one similar program is GoodRx—and one may argue that giving Amazon information about your medications adds another layer to privacy concerns. However, the benefit is free if you do decide to use it, and it may be worth checking out if you pay a lot out of pocket for prescription medications.

There's another health benefit called OneMedical that includes access to same- and next-day appointments on certain virtual-care services for things like common colds, allergies, yeast infections, or urinary tract infections. It costs $99 per year. Your insurance provider may offer a similar program.

Amazon Key offers select Prime members in-garage delivery. If you live in an eligible area and you're interested, you'll need to purchase and install a smart garage kit. Amazon Key previously offered in-home delivery, but that service is currently on pause. (Of course, this also comes with a slew of privacy concerns.)

There are three different Amazon credit cards. These come in the form of rewards back for Prime members on select purchases or at select retailers. You don't need to get an Amazon credit card to make use of Prime benefits. In fact, I encourage you to read through all of the available information and carefully consider it before deciding whether or not to get a credit card.
